summary:
La Libertad region stands under Peru's national framework. Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents requires restroom entry to be determined by 'biological sex', barring trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their gender identity, and the same package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'. Vague child-protection articles in that law, including a ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, leaving Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected, and its co-author, trans journalist and human-rights defender Gianna Camacho, stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry; between 2020 and 2023, 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed. In December 2025 three police officers were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history. Two protective developments are on record: in June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, and in July 2025 a Lima constitutional court ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

La Libertad appears in the Public Ministry's Observatory of Criminality study of intentional deaths of LGTB people in Peru between 2012 and 2021, which recorded 84 criminal complaints involving 88 victims and 72 identified suspects. Fifty-eight per cent of the deaths were concentrated in six fiscal districts: Lima (12), La Libertad (10), Lima Norte (10), Lima Este (7), Lima Sur (6) and Callao (6). La Libertad therefore ranks second in absolute count, level with Lima Norte and behind Lima, making it one of the two highest-burden jurisdictions outside the capital.

The Regional Government of La Libertad adopted Ordenanza Regional N.° 009-2024-GRLL-CR of 6 September 2024, promoting labour inclusion of travesti, transsexual and transgender persons in the region. It declares that every such person has the right to formal, dignified and productive work in equitable and satisfactory conditions without discrimination on grounds of gender identity and/or its expression, and recognises the trans community as a group in a situation of vulnerability in La Libertad.
tangentialFactors:
The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru found that the bathroom provision openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by barring access to facilities matching their gender identity, implicitly framing them as harassment risks, and recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.

Enforcement of the national restriction reaches private and public life. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy, and on television presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

The regional ordinance grounds itself in Peru's constitutional equality guarantees and article 323 of the Penal Code, under which discrimination is a crime, and recalls a 2014 regional-council session framework against discrimination on sexual orientation and gender identity. Set against that, the national hate-crime regime carries no LGBT coverage after the 2017 repeal, which was carried by Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures.
localsOnly:
Ordenanza Regional N.° 000009-2024-GRLL-CR was presented in the regional council's ordinary session of 3 September 2024, debated, approved and signed in Trujillo on 6 September 2024, and published in El Peruano on 7 November 2024, entering into force the day after publication. Its object is positive-action measures for the effective labour inclusion of travesti, transsexual and transgender persons in La Libertad.

The ordinance orders the establishment of a working group (mesa de trabajo) to carry the measures forward and recommends that local governments in La Libertad issue municipal ordinances recognising gender identity and fundamental rights. Residents of La Libertad are therefore covered by a regional instrument that expressly names them as a vulnerable group entitled to non-discriminatory access to formal work.

The Public Ministry's study was developed with the Justice Ministry human-rights office and the University Cayetano Heredia LGTB-rights observatory with UNDP support, and yielded recommendations including training criminal prosecutors on LGTB-victim identification and improving monitoring systems.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not resolve whether any municipal ordinances of the type recommended by Ordenanza Regional N.° 009-2024-GRLL-CR have been issued by districts within La Libertad, or whether the ordered working group has been convened and what it has produced. These are unresolved points, not established facts either way.

Whether the April 2025 national restroom restriction has been applied or challenged within La Libertad's public facilities is not sourced here. The only documented enforcement example in the inventory is the dismissal of a complaint against a gym, which took place through a consumer-protection body and is not attributed to La Libertad.

Whether the labour-inclusion ordinance has produced measurable changes in hiring or discrimination complaints in La Libertad is not sourced. The homicide figures date from a 2022 study covering 2012 to 2021 and are not updated to the present, and the sub-registry caveat attached to national hate-crime counts applies equally to any count drawn from La Libertad.
